Mr. Speaker, this is an amendment to subsection 1 of section 5 of the act respecting the Revised Statutes of Canada which was adopted during the session of 1947-48. The amendment provides for the addition of the following words:
-and whenever in the said statutes or acts, or amendments thereto, the expression "Dominion of Canada" is used, there shall be substituted therefor the expression "Canada", and whenever the word "Dominion" is used, there shall be substituted therefor the word "Canada" or "Canadian or "federal", respectively, or such other adequate word as the context requires.
The reason for this amendment is obvious. It is to be found in the fact that since Canada has ceased to be a dominion and has become a sovereign state, the word "dominion" as applied to Canada has lost its meaning, and-

speechtext:
Last Tuesday the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I., (Mr. McLure) asked a question concerning the site of the proposed new

building in Charlottetown. His question was, in part:
When will the department or the government make a definite statement about these properties, so that these land owners, home owners and tenants can make arrangements for other locations in the future?
I see I made quite a short answer. I said: "As soon as possible." I think in fairness to the hon. member I should give him the following details.
Notice of expropriation was filed against properties contained in the city block bounded by Richmond street, Pownall street, Sidney street and Queen street in Charlottetown in March of this year, these properties comprising the site selected for the new public building.
Valuations have been obtained on these properties, compiled by Mr. P. S. Bradley and Mr. Gilbert Gaudet of Charlottetown, and the owners communicated with in regard to negotiations for settlements for the properties. No settlements have yet been made, because the asking prices are much in excess of our valuations. The department is now arranging for a third valuation, and upon receipt of this valuation the owners will be communicated with again.
The chief architect has stated that vacant possession of the properties will be required for April 1, 1950, and it is the intention to have notices to vacate by that date forwarded to the former owners at once. In the meantime, negotiations towards settlements for the acquisition of these properties will be continued.

POLLUTION
subsubtopic: CONTROL OF INDUSTRIAL PLANTS AND OIL REFINERIES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
Navigable Waters Protection Act
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendment concerns two principles. The first is the protection of the riparian rights of persons dwelling on or using the banks of navigable streams or lakes. The second is the democratic principle of the greatest good for the greatest number. The terms of the present act as to pollution definitely give the minister limited authority. The limitation of the present statute is that it proscribes and prohibits the pollution of navigable waters by the depositing of any sawdust, edgings, slabs, bark or rubbish of any description whatsoever into any river, stream or other water, any part of which is navigable or which flows into any navigable water. That provision is to be found in the present Navigable Waters Protection Act, section 19, chapter 140 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. It definitely establishes the right of the federal parliament to deal with matters concerning navigable waters, and waters running into navigable waters.
The amendment that I propose for the consideration of the house today is merely an enlargement of the description of the methods of pollution of navigable waters. The bill is in almost identical words with the original act, and includes such substances as oil, sawdust, chemicals or other industrial pollution. The amendment to section 19 reads:
No owner, lessee, or person operating any industrial plant, oil refinery, chemical works, sawmill or other plant or works, or any other person, shall discharge or throw or allow to be discharged or thrown any noxious waste product, oil. sawdust, chemical or other matter or thing into a river, stream or other water any part of which is navigable or which flows into any navigable water, which has the effect of polluting the water into which it enters or is liable to pollute such waters.
In the same phraseology as the original act, it merely enlarges the description of the methods of pollution. In my opinion it does not alter, substantially or otherwise, the powers and the jurisdiction of the federal parliament; nor is it in any way ultra vires of the rights of the federal parliament because of the overriding rights of any provincial parliament.
In this connection a case has recently been decided in the Supreme Court of Canada which has a definite bearing on the amendment I am introducing in the house today. I am going to quote certain salient paragraphs of the judgments rendered by the Supreme Court of Ontario, in both trial and appellate divisions, and by the Supreme Court of Canada, which judgment was rendered only the day before yesterday. The case is known as McKie v. the K.V.P. Company Limited. Briefly, the company was sued by the owners of riparian rights on the Spanish

Navigable Waters Protection Act river, who sought damages as a result of the pollution of the waters of that river. The first judgment had this to say:
The proprietor of riparian lands has a right incident to the land, independent of ownership of the solum of the stream or river, to the flow of water through or by his land in its natural state, and if the stream is polluted or otherwise interfered with so as to affect this right, by an upper riparian proprietor (who has not yet acquired a prescriptive right so to interfere), the lower proprietor may maintain an action for an injunction without proving damage, which is presumed from the interference with the right. It is immaterial, in such an action, that the defendant carries on a business which is important to the community, and carries it on in a proper manner, nor are the economic necessities of the defendant relevant to be considered.
The second paragraph of the judgment reads:
Where smells arise from a river, caused by the effluent entering the water from a mill, and are so offensive as to be an actual and substantial interference with the comfort and enjoyment of properties on the river, measured by ordinary and reasonable standards, and consequently what has been an attractive resort for tourists becomes much less desirable, the owners of the properties are entitled to relief on the footing of nuisance, as well as to relief based on the interference with their riparian rights.
In this case the learned judge awarded damages and also granted an injunction; and it is with the injunction in particular I wish to deal at the present time. The learned judge had this to say:
On all the evidence I find as a fact that the waters of the Spanish river below the defendant's plant have been polluted by the defendant in such a manner as to change their character and substantially affect the use to which the plaintiffs were entitled to put them and to interfere with the enjoyment of the plaintiffs as occupiers of riparian lands.
In his judgment the judge also went back to the common law:
The origin of the common law applicable to this subject goes back to and beyond the Roman law.
The judgment goes on to state clearly the rights of riparian ownership, but I need not add to the quotations I have already given. It awarded certain sums of money to the plaintiffs, and also-and this is the important point -granted an injunction prohibiting the company from continuing the practice of dumping this effluent into the Spanish river. The injunction is in these terms:
An injunction will go restraining the defendant from depositing foreign substances or matter in the Spanish river which alter the character or quality of the water flowing over the lands of the plaintiff . . .
The important point in that judgment is that the learned judge based his decision upon the alteration of the quality of the water. That judgment was taken to the appellate division of the Supreme Court of Ontario,

where the appeal was dismissed and the judgment sustained. In dismissing the appeal the chief justice had this to say:
It is no defence to the person who pollutes to show that the waters were already polluted by other persons. Nor is it a defence that the pollution is the result of business operations carried on in a proper manner and that the business is important to the community.
This judgment was rendered by Chief Justice Robertson, with Justices Laidlaw and Aylesworth concurring. The judgment sustains the damages awarded in the first action and also continues the injunction in these words:
This court doth order and adjudge that the defendant be, and it is hereby, restrained from depositing foreign substances or matter in the Spanish river which alter the character or quality of the water washing the lands owned or occupied by the plaintiff . . .
This court doth order and adjudge that the defendant be, and it is hereby, restrained from discharging or permitting to be discharged from the defendant's works mentioned in the pleadings, into the waters of the Spanish river, any substance or matter that, to the injury of the plaintiff, affects the quality or character of the waters of the said river where the plaintiff's lands border upon it, or that causes the said waters to become less pure than otherwise they would be.
These judgments contain voluminous references both to the common law and to decisions of the privy council, and are in the strongest possible legal terms.
After that judgment was rendered the Ontario act was altered, and an appeal was taken to the Supreme Court of Canada, in which the decision was rendered only the day before yesterday.

subsubtopic: CONTROL OF INDUSTRIAL PLANTS AND OIL REFINERIES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? In what manner has the Ontario act been amended?

subtopic: POLLUTION
subsubtopic: CONTROL OF INDUSTRIAL PLANTS AND OIL REFINERIES
speechtext:
I will give the minister that information. It was amended to prevent an injunction being imposed against an industrial plant. There were qualifications to that amendment, but that was the substance of it.
To continue with the supreme court judgment, Mr. Justice Kerwin says:
The sole point argued before us was as to the injunction.
The learned justices say that the injunction shall stand, despite the amendment to the Ontario statute. It was because of the alteration to the Ontario act that counsel for the company appealed and said the injunction should not stand. The supreme court decided, however, that because the case had come to trial before the Ontario statute was amended, the original judgment with regard to the injunction should stand.
I quote from the supreme court judgment:
The amended act came into force on the day it received the royal assent, April 1, 1949, and while the judgment of the court of appeal was given

November 22, 1948, it is contended that the appeal to this court is "pending" within the meaning of the enactment.
May 1 clear up a point by quoting from the judgment?
. . . and since a provincial legislature may not extend the jurisdiction of this court as conferred by parliament, such a provision as the one here in question would not, even if it purported so to do, enable this court to give a judgment that was impossible in law at the time of the decision of the court of appeal.
The reason for the appeal, briefly, was that this company felt seriously aggrieved by the injunction. An alteration in the law was sought which would permit a company causing pollution or distress to riparian owners to pay those riparian owners for the distress so caused. The company could, at the same time, continue the practice which caused those damages. In other words, companies operating on a river could continue to pollute the stream as long as they continued to pay damages to the people inconvenienced by that pollution. Not being a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, I am unable to say whether or not that is a good principle of law. I do know it is not a good principle of ethics, and it is not a good principle from the humanitarian point of view.
The supreme court said:
The rights of riparian owners have always been zealously guarded by the courts.
The learned judges quoted from a privy council decision by Lord Sumner which reads as follows:
The grant of an injunction is the proper remedy for a violation of right, according to a current of authority, which is of many years' standing and is practically unbroken.
There is one more decision of the privy council to which reference is made in this judgment. It is a decision by Viscount Finlay, Lord Birkenhead, and Lord Dunedin. It says in part:
. . . the courts have on more than one occasion expressed their determination to prevent any abuse of the act by legalizing the commission of torts by any defendant who was able and willing to pay damages.
There are quotations from several other cases, all to the same effect. The basic rule is that the injunction shall stand.
So far as I am able to ascertain, Mr. Speaker, that is the legal position in this case. The Ontario act has been amended; so it would seem to me that the sole protector of riparian rights on navigable waters, and waters running into navigable streams, is the federal parliament. The wording of section 19 of the act is to that effect; therefore I believe I am borne out in my contentions.
We come now, sir, to the question of possible damage to industry through this bill which I have introduced. I am informed that
Navigable Waters Protection Act most of the states in the northern United States have enacted similar legislation to that which I am requesting with regard to the pollution of streams. The question of the rights of industry versus the rights of the people is one that should receive careful study. Obviously it would be harmful if an act were passed by this parliament enforcing such restrictions against the pulp and paper industry and others who are not discharging an effluent which damages any riparian owners. It would be wrong, by such an act, so to prescribe their actions and their operations that it would become difficult or impossible for them to continue. I believe that the terms of my amendment are sufficiently flexible to give the power to the minister and the board of transport commissioners to decide each case on its merits. It is left to the good judgment of the court to decide whether or not damage was done.
There again we come to the question of the greatest good for the greatest number. Obviously that is not a legal point, but certainly it is an ethical point; and it is one of the fundamental points of democracy. Obviously it would be wrong to put into any statute something which would cause unemployment or restrict the development of the pulp and paper industry. But, sir, in this case, where there was abundant evidence of pollution that made this river completely and absolutely unusable, the courts have decided that there should be an injunction directing that such pollution should cease.
I want to speak briefly about one other industry which I know something about, and which also has a problem in connection with effluent disposal. I refer to the mining industry. Tailings or slimes containing cyanide-the waste rock or the waste mill products-must be disposed of in some way The practice has been to dump these tailings into a lake, and in some cases damage has no doubt been done to the lakes so treated. But although several mines have dumped tailings into Red lake-and I have a letter to this effect on my desk at the moment-the Ashing and bathing in that lake have not been seriously interfered with because of pollution. Therefore that type of industrial pollution, while not to be recommended, is nevertheless not in the same class as that with which the learned justices of the supreme court dealt in the case of K.V.P. v. McKie. I am quite sure that the mining industry can in the future build its mills so that the tailings and the slimes can in most cases be deposited on land and not dumped into the waters of surrounding lakes. In many cases slimes can perform the useful service of providing a firebreak around the property so that mines built in the bush can provide themselves

Navigable Waters Protection Act with a ring of fire protection around the camp. As a matter of fact that is what is being done at the present time in Kirkland Lake. We must also take into consideration the fact that all these industrial processes are constantly improving and developing. I am informed that it is the modern practice of kraft mills such as K.V.P. to store their fibre effluent which causes damage, and to burn this effluent after a period of leaching or drying. I am told that in some kraft mills in the United States this product actually provides heat and power for the mills for several days a month. In the case that I have referred to it was stated that some four or five tons of these fibres were discharged every day into the Spanish river, and the evidence given was to the effect that this material could be dried and burned. I am not competent to pass judgment on that matter, but the information was given to me by an engineer whose opinion I esteem.
So much for the law; so much for the possibility of proscribing and restraining industrial development because of this bill. Now we come to the real reason why I have introduced this measure to this house.
During the summer of this year,.because of pollution, by oil slick and other noxious substances, of the water along the shore of lake Ontario for several miles in the vicinity of Toronto, the use of all the beaches in my riding-and I understand of the beaches elsewhere also-was prohibited by orders of the medical officers of health in the respective municipalities. The use of Sunnyside beach, Long Branch beach, the beaches at the east end of Toronto, at New Toronto, and in Mimico-all teeming with bathers and swimmers from the industrial centres immediately behind them-was completely prohibited during that period by the medical officers of health, because of the pollution, generally considered to be caused by oil, which had taken place. Pictures were published showing, at Sunnyside beach-probably the most densely populated beach in all of Canada-bathers attempting to go into the water and coming out with their feet dripping with oil sludge and pollution.
Here again the principle of the greatest good for the greatest number should apply. A population of a million people were prevented, during one of the longest hot spells we have ever experienced-for a period not of days but weeks-from using their beaches and their lakes because of industrial pollution. This is a situation which, in my opinion, the parliament of Canada should not tolerate- and parliament is the competent authority to deal with it. Attempts were made to trace the source of this pollution. One of the suspected sources refused to admit anyone to
[Mr. Adamson.}

its premises to ascertain the cause, or the suspected cause of the lake pollution, and under the present law apparently no remedial action was possible.
So much for the pollution with regard to human rights; besides that, Mr. Speaker, a great number of wildfowl were killed by the oil lying on the water, and the conservation authorities were much distressed about it. In addition, numerous small craft were seriously incommoded by the oil slime which fouled their bottoms. The smell of the oil, or whatever it was, caused putrefaction of marine growth, and in itself was offensive until the entire lake shore became a malodorous place, the conditions being similar to those on the Spanish river. This, again, is a condition which in this day and age, in this day of better living, should not be tolerated by a modern state.
But there is one more thing. The oil slick was considered to be a serious fire hazard. Fortunately it did not catch fire, but I understand that the fire authorities in Toronto took what they considered to be necessary precautions, and were greatly concerned lest it should catch fire; statements to that effect were made throughout the press of Toronto and the surrounding districts. Therefore on that ground I believe that this industrial pollution should be stopped.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this is an instance in which a million people have suffered owing to the pollution of that part of lake Ontario.
We come now to the suggested remedies. The amendment I have introduced gives the minister power to inspect any installation or industry, oil refinery, chemical plant or other works situated on or near a navigable water or a stream entering into that navigable water. This merely means that the minister may, as happened this summer, if the residents of the district are suspicious that a certain industrial plant is polluting the water, send an inspector into that plant to see that the plant is operated in such a way as not to cause pollution of the water. It is reasonable to suggest that this be done. If the plant in question is not polluting the water, nothing is done. If the plant in question is polluting the water, the minister may put in inspectors, or may require the burning or other disposal of the waste product which is being discharged into the lake; or he may take other measures which he and his inspectors, who will be technically trained men, deem to be necessary and proper. If the industry considers that it is not being fairly treated, the appeal, as in all cases, will be to the board of transport commissioners. I feel that that is a necessary qualification in this act. Apparently at the present time, under the Ontario

statutes, you can dump anything into lake Ontario and there is nobody to say you nay. If anybody sues you for damage under riparian rights, he can collect small damages, but you cannot prevent the industry in question from continuing to pollute the lake. This is indefensible. I suggest that the amendment I have introduced does not injure any industry which is not polluting the water; nor does it injure any industry that has a proper method of waste disposal.
I come now to the next part of the bill, which concerns sewage disposal. It may surprise hon. members to know that a great number of the larger cities of Canada do in fact discharge raw and untreated sewage right into the rivers or lakes. I understand that the capital city of Ottawa is one of the greatest offenders in this regard. I am also informed that the city of Montreal has no sewage disposal plant. The house will remember the violence of the expressions used some years ago with regard to sewage disposal in Chicago, and that the United States authorities required Chicago to install sewage disposal plants at considerable cost. The city of Chicago did in fact install sewage disposal plants. It seems to me that this whole question of sewage disposal requires a great deal more consideration than it has been given up to the present time.

Yes.

The proper disposal of sewage is a matter requiring the attention of all levels of government, because in many ways it is expensive to install a sewage disposal plant. However, modern sewage disposal plants have been found to be good investments, and modern practice has shown that they can be made to pay their way.
During the summer the concentration of colon bacillus increases as the year goes on, generally reaching the maximum late in August or early in September. It is significant that the curve of the incidence of poliomyelitis almost follows the curve of the increase in concentration of colon bacillus. This is not to say that the colon bacillus is responsible for poliomyelitis, but there is at least circumstantial evidence that this killing disease has an affinity for colon bacillus.
Navigable Waters Protection Act
Sewage oxidizes with the turbulence of a river, and tends to dilute and become less dangerous, provided that the concentration in the first instance is not too great. However, if it is too great that does not occur, and the sewage continues to be a menace for many miles down the river. The Ottawa river is a case in point; the sewage discharged by the city of Ottawa causes much discomfort and is a menace to health for a considerable stretch along the river below the city. So much for sewage disposal.
In this bill the penalties are increased above those in the original bill. There has been a decrease in the value of money, and I felt that the penalties for breaches should be increased.
Water is one of Canada's most sacred trusts. The North American continent has three-quarters of the fresh water of the world. A citizen from any other continent coming to North America is impressed by the abundance of fresh water, particularly when he comes to Canada. It is an inheritance which we must guard.
No other country is dependent upon water to the extent that Canada is. No other country develops so much power from water, and no other country uses it to the extent that we do for navigation. In no other country is it put to so much use as a tourist attraction. It seems to me it is the fundamental duty of this parliament and of the whole Canadian people to preserve, maintain and conserve the rivers and lakes of the country as a sacred trust. This is the overriding reason for the introduction of this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the hon. gentleman to some of the features of this bill. I am sorry I did not have an opportunity to confer with the hon. gentleman. I did not know this bill was coming up until five minutes to three, although he sent a note to my office at 1.40 p.m. I have conferred with the law clerk about the bill. I admit that the bill has a laudable object. I should like to quote a letter which I wrote to the mayor of Toronto, Hiram E. McCallum, in connection with this matter, as follows:
I forward to you eight copies of Bill No. 6, introduced by Mr. Rodney Adamson, M.P., in the House of Commons, which is up for first reading in the house tonight. Sept. 27.
A letter was also sent to Dr. Ollivier, Law Clerk of the House of Commons, before the bill was up for second reading. The letter reads in part:
You will note by the bill, as I see it, that if such a bill passes it will prevent the city from using Coatsworth Cut and pouring the liquids from the main drainage works into lake Ontario accordingly.

Navigable Waters Protection Act
You may remember that the Don river used to flow into Toronto bay. Then the city spent $30 million on harbour improvements, including the viaduct which now runs across the front of the city. I want to commend the hon. gentleman for introducing this bill, but I should like to call his attention to one feature of it. As I have said, I wrote to Dr. Ollivier, Law Clerk of the House of Commons, who is learned in this subject and has written a textbook. The letter continues:
You might also note that the Globe and Mail in an editorial last Friday approved of the Adamson bill, as did an editorial in the Toronto Telegram of Monday. October 3, although the bill will prevent the city of Toronto from pouring any liquids into lake Ontario. The city spent $50 million on a duplicate intake pipe.
The people of the riding of the hon. member who is proposing this amendment are using that water. It is pure water, and when you turn on the tap it is cold. It is filtered and chlorinated. As much water as would fill this chamber would need only a small quantity of chlorine, about the size of an ink stand.
The city spent $50 million on a duplicate intake pipe off Scarborough beach, and the plans were passed by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier). Before the city of Toronto started this $50 million project at Scarborough they applied, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, to the Minister of Public Works, who must sanction the plans and specifications. After proper notice the various authorities came down here and the minister issued the necessary permit to proceed with the plant.
I want to call your attention to the size of Toronto harbour today, because there are some new members in the house. Under the new definition, Toronto harbour starts at the centre of the Humber river, the dividing line between the city of Toronto and the township, and runs straight south of the Humber river out into lake Ontario for a distance of three miles, thence east about a mile and a half off Toronto island to a point off Woodbine avenue. Woodbine avenue is as far as the harbour improvement runs on the east. Thence it runs inland. That is the new definition of the harbour, and the harbour authorities have the power to prevent pollution in that territory. A lot of money was spent, and the plans were passed by the Minister of Public Works.
The letter to the mayor of Toronto continues as follows:
. . . and formerly we only had one intake pipe off Gibraltar point, Toronto island-
Near the Sick Children's hospital.
-which had not been inspected for thirty-five years. It blew up in 1910 and 1911, and the city was compelled to drink water from lake Ontario, through

a tunnel from the lake off Toronto island, thence north to Long pond to the shore tunnel at Mugg's landing, Toronto island, and thence across Toronto bay to the pumping station at the foot of John street.
This civic water is pure water, filtered by the slow sand filtration method at the filtration plant on Toronto island and under chlorination of a small amount.. The water is always cold, and we have had hardly any diphtheria or typhoid fever since.
The city built a duplicate intake system costing about $50 million at Victoria park, and has been giving city water to large sections of the county of York to the east, north and west of the city limits proper. These outside places are also being allowed to use Toronto's greatly overtaxed sewage disposal main drainage works in front of the Woodbine race track, where the liquids only are poured after the diversion of the Don river through Coatsworth Cut into lake Ontario accordingly.
I have not had the opportunity yet of conferring with Mr. Adamson about his bill. It also deals with the Don river. As I was born near the banks of the river Don, I know something about that river. There has always been sewage poured into the Don, in my opinion.
Dr. Ollivier, Law Clerk of the House of Commons, gave his opinion on the bill. In my letter to the mayor of the city of Toronto I said:
In my opinion the bill is so worded as to prevent the city from pouring any liquids into lake Ontario in the future, although the city had its plans passed under the Navigable Waters Protection Act by the Minister of Public Works before going ahead with the Scarborough plant. These outside places are also using Toronto's greatly overtaxed sewage disposal works from your main drainage works in front of the Woodbine race track. I shall be glad to give you any further information you wish on the subject.
Dr. Ollivier's opinion is as follows:
If you will so authorize me, I would bring your letter to the attention of Mr. Adamson, with whom I have co-operated in the preparation of his bill.
You will notice that I was careful to provide that not only should noxious products not be discharged in navigable waters but also in all streams or waters which flow into any navigable water.
It is true, as you state, that the Toronto harbour commission has the right to pass bylaws and rules and regulations preventing pollution of waters within their boundary-
That is the new boundary which I explained a few minutes ago.
-and therefore it would not be a bad idea to make it clear that the prescription applies to them as well as to any municipality, although I imagine that the words "any other person shall . . . allow to be discharged . . ." would cover the case.
As to the city of Toronto, they would by the bill be prevented from pouring their liquids at Coatsworth Cut, etc.
It is the opinion of the law clerk, and I gave him the same opinion some time ago, that the city of Toronto would be prevented from doing so by the bill. They would be prevented from pouring liquids into Coatsworth Cut, and using the main drainage works accordingly.
I am sorry to have to take this stand, because I believe that the hon. member had a laudable objective in mind in bringing his

proposal before the house. As you know, Toronto harbour is now fenced off. I remember when the people of Toronto used to be able to bathe at the beaches at Parkdale and all over Toronto island, and at the eastern beaches. That was before the harbour improvement began, but the harbour improvement fenced it off, and there was only one bathing place. They constructed a bath house at Sunnyside which cost $400,000. I did not believe in it myself, and I voted against it when the matter was before the harbour board. I was then mayor, and we were told if we did not proceed with the plan they would stop the work at Ottawa. They spent $400,000 on a bath house at Sunnyside, but the water of the lake is always too cold for the bathers. The result was that the city had to build a very large open air swimming pool at Sunnyside to the east of the bath house. The water of this pool is chlorinated and filtered and is always at a temperature of not less than sixty-five degrees.
When members of the House of Commons visited Toronto last April they saw it, but it was not opened until May. X wish they could have seen it in the summertime, but we hope to have them come to see us again. We hope that some members will be coming up to attend the winter fair.
I do not know that there is anything more I can say about the bill. I do not wish to detain the house longer, but I want to point out that the city of Toronto has been most just and generous to these outlying municipalities. They not only give them water, but they also allow them to use the main drainage works. Otherwise some of those municipalities, which are not very well off, would have had to build their own water plants, and they would be getting their water in the same way as they do in other cities where diphtheria and typhoid are more prevalent.
In 1910 the old intake at Toronto island broke up. I was on the board of control in 1910. They tried for two years to raise the original intake pipe off Gibraltar point, which is near the Sick Children's hospital. Then I got Mr. Robert Weddell, senior, of Trenton, who built the western entrance to Toronto harbour, and Captain John Manley. They went out there at seven o'clock in the morning. They said that the principle that had been followed in trying to raise the broken intake pipe off Toronto island by pontoons was all wrong. I was opposed to that myself, and the powerful Toronto Telegram came to our support. Mr. Weddell and Captain Manley went out with two scows, and a diver went down. One scow was placed on each side of the broken intake pipe; the diver put cables at both ends of that pipe and after about five
Navigable Waters Protection Act hours work it was hauled up to a scow and afterwards brought to the foot of John street. It was repaired in about ten days and replaced in the original position off Toronto island.
That shows what can be done by an efficient public works department. Public leaders may be here today and gone tomorrow, and the key to good municipal government is to have good heads of departments. During the seven years I was in office in Toronto, with the exception of one or two departments, I doubt if I discussed matters in their own offices with the heads of the various departments of that city. They had full authority in regard to policy and full authority to appoint their staffs. I never interfered.
I commend the hon. gentleman Mr. Adamson on the good work he has done, because he has been a most valuable member of this house; but I would ask that he allow this bill to stand until he has conferred with officials of the city of Toronto. I do not want to prevent anyone from speaking on the bill today; far from it. I would ask the hon. gentleman, however, to consider the Toronto angle. Throughout his riding they are using that drinking water. It is pure and cold, chlorinated and filtered. They also use the sewage disposal works; otherwise they would have to provide their own water supply and sewage works, at great expense. The city of Toronto has been most just and generous, and I believe many other cities could adopt the method followed by that great city. It is a great city, though we have no ministers representing it in the cabinet. Now, however, we have some young Liberal members of parliament on the government side coming from Toronto, and I hope they will study this bill and help look after the interests of that city.
While I commend the young member for his good intentions and good works, I would remind him as well as hon. gentlemen opposite that you can never answer a newspaper; it always has the last word. I believe the newspapers had a worthy object in view in endeavouring to give the people of Toronto some of the bathing beaches they had in the old days, but I regret to say that the way they have attempted to attain their objective does not meet the needs of the case.

believe the hon. member who introduced this bill put forth a sincere effort, and perhaps had a real grievance, but I should like to refer very briefly to one or two points in connection with it. This bill proposes to repeal section 19 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act. If we read that section closely we will see that it deals with the physical aspects of

Navigable Waters Protection Act navigation, with the turning of propellers, the obstruction to ships, and so on. If we read the proposed section 19 (1), however, it all boils down to the pollution of the water. I suggest that the amendment takes away the real meaning of the original section 19, dealing with the physical aspects of navigation; and we all realize that the act then would be incomplete, because a ship could still travel in polluted waters. That is the first comment I have to offer, and I suggest that the present section 19 should remain as it is.
No one likes a drink of pure water better than I do, but I think we must look at this from the standpoint of the greatest good to the greatest number. I live in Kingston, which is an old, historic city. Some of the newer places may consider us a little old-fashioned, because our sewage is still poured into lake Ontario where it enters the St. Lawrence river. Occasionally we have complaints as far as the water is concerned; but if this bill were adopted I suggest it would work a great hardship on the ratepayers of Kingston and other municipalities similarly situated, which dispose of their sewage in that way. I am sure the number of ratepayers who would be adversely affected would be much greater than the number of people who would benefit, because the adoption of this bill would require the immediate installation of sewage disposal plants.
In his amendment the hon. member has suggested some remedies. I do not believe they would be sufficient to give proper guidance to those who might be administering this legislation. Furthermore I believe this is a matter which should be left to the province, since it concerns property and civil rights.
I suggest that it has been brought up in the wrong house. Section 2 of the proposed bill reads:
The said act is further amended by adding immediately after section twenty-six the following section:
"26A. (1) The minister may, if he has reason to believe that an industrial plant is likely to discharge noxious substances into navigable waters, or into any river, stream or other water which flows into any navigable water, appoint inspectors, empowered to reside at the plant and report any violation of the provisions of the act. The cost of maintaining such inspectors shall be chargeable against and a debt owing the crown by the owner, lessee or operator of the plant."
I think that is definitely a matter of property and civil rights, and I suggest this parliament is not empowered to pass any measure of that kind. So while I agree with the principle put forward by the hon. member,
I suggest that at the present time this bill is premature as far as the older municipalities are concerned, such as Kingston, Belleville, Napanee and so on. I believe it is a proper

Mr. Speaker, the constituency I have the honour to represent is very much interested in the bill which has been introduced in this house by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson). My constituency consists of the city of Windsor and the contiguous township of Sandwich West. It is situated at the junction of lake St. Clair and the Detroit river, which incidentally is the busiest inland waterway in the world. South of that, there is lake Erie. You can see, therefore, that the pollution of waters is a matter of great importance to us; and many worthy local organizations have been studying this problem for some time.
At this time, I should like to pay tribute to the valuable work of the international joint commission. The facts that it has uncovered and the recommendations it has made from time to time for the correction of the pollution of fresh waters have proven very valuable to my constituents. I should like to be associated with that a tribute to one who sat in this chamber, the Hon. James Glen. He also served as Minister of Mines and Resources and is now chairman of the international joint commission. The constituency of Essex West appreciates the work he has done.
Many public and semi-public bodies have taken a great deal of interest in assisting the different governmental organizations in uncovering the facts. One of these organizations is the Essex County Sportsmen's Association. I have before me two telegrams, one from Mr. L. Albrough, the president, and the other from the secretary-treasurer, Mr. S. E. Chauvin, in which they have asked me to support the bill on behalf of the 1,800 members of that particular branch of the sportsmen's association. It is their feeling that this is a step in the right direction. The members of the association are deeply interested in this work and have, therefore, asked me to support the bill.
For reasons which I shall give later, I do not think that this is the proper time to support such a measure. I do, however, believe the principle of the bill is a laudable one which should be supported by all hon. members. For the reasons that have been given by the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Henderson), and which I imagine will be given by the Minister of Transport in due course, I do not believe this is the proper place to introduce such a measure.
In my constituency we are deeply concerned about the pollution of navigable fresh waters. The Essex County Sportsmen's

Association has done a great deal, as I have said, to uncover the facts concerning this matter. As a matter of fact, this summer that organization took me on a tour of the Detroit river, showing me a place where a particular corporation is now pumping refuse from the United States and dumping it on an island in that river. It is the claim of the experts who accompanied us on this trip that the refuse being dumped on this island has caused the foliage, weeds, and things of that nature in the area to dry up and disappear. This, of course, has caused the disappearance of the fish and wildlife from that area. I am drawing this to the attention of the government because permission was given recently for the installation of additional pipe lines to carry this refuse from the United States. The chemicals from the refuse which has accumulated in piles on the island are flowing into the stream.
The city of Windsor has, I understand, made plans for the treating of the sewage from the city and adjacent towns. There are other sources of pollution. A rather serious case was brought to our attention recently in which one of the public utilities was allowing oil to enter what is known as the river Canard. This oil became ignited and killed thousands of dollars' worth of fish, muskrat and other game. I do not propose to deal with the legal aspects of the matter, because that will be ably handled at a later time. Many people, and particularly those who have riparian rights, have suffered considerable damage because of the pollution of these waters, not only in the streams I have mentioned but in many others as well. We must consider, however, the place from which relief should be sought, and my opinion is that this measure should have been introduced in the legislature of the province of Ontario.
The introduction of this bill has value in that it will provide publicity for this particular question, the pollution of fresh water, not only in my constituency but throughout the whole of Canada. It will provide a subject of conversation and will arouse the Canadian people generally to the great harm being done innocently by industries in the pollution of these streams. Large commercial corporations will also learn of the loss they are suffering in permitting this refuse to go into these rivers. Some of this refuse has a high commercial value. Without giving too many illustrations, I may say that I have been told by experts of several cases in the Detroit river and lake St. Clair area in which, after investigation, the industries in question were told how to eliminate the pollution of
Navigable Waters Protection Act the water and, at the same time, derive considerable commercial value from the refuse that had been dumped in the river.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this bill has had some value in the publicity which will be given the subject. For the reasons I have stated I cannot support the bill, but I can commend the principle of it to the Canadian people.

I am fortunate enough, Mr. Speaker, to represent the riding of Parkdale in Toronto. I say "fortunate" advisedly since I am the first Liberal to represent that riding since confederation.
I have listened with great interest and with great respect to the argument for and the clear explanation of the bill placed before the house by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson). My riding of Parkdale fronts on lake Ontario, and at the south of it is Sunny-side beach. As has been stated by the hon. member for York West, that beach was covered with oil for most of the summer. I could hardly help being in complete sympathy with the motivation behind the first section of this bill. While my sympathy is there, however, what little reason I possess tells me that we are in the wrong jurisdiction. I would suggest with respect, and I have not made a constitutional study of this bill, that the dominion, under section 91 of the British North America Act, has jurisdiction over navigation and shipping; and that, accordingly, unless we are dealing with the matter of navigation and shipping, we are dealing with something which is not within the legislative powers of this parliament.
In the bill presented here, it would appear to be a fairly clear case of trying to prevent pollution. It is possible that pollution might affect navigation and shipping. I can conceive of pollution being so heavy and so burdensome that it would cover the bottom of a river or canal to the point that navigation might be difficult or impossible. But until such a thing happens or is in danger of happening-and again I offer this opinion with the greatest respect to the hon. members of this house-I personally feel that the matter would not come under navigation and shipping. Possibly also, if the liquid became so thick that it hindered navigation to the point that it lessened the normal speed of vessels, it might be considered under navigation and shipping. While I not only sympathize with the motives behind this bill, and only wish it were possible for us to pass a bill of this kind, in so far as section 1 of it is concerned, I nevertheless submit with respect that this parliament has no jurisdiction.

Navigable Waters Protection Act
As to section 2 of the bill-and at this stage I am not proposing to go into the particulars of the sections; I am dealing with the bill generally-I would welcome it with the greatest of delight. It would give the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) the power to send inspectors into the industries throughout Canada for the purpose of preventing pollution, and the industries in question would pay the salaries of those inspectors. That is a delightful dream that we politicians have had for many years. I can just conceive of the minister sending thousands and thousands of Liberal devotees into the industries of Canada, and having those industries pay for those inspectors. This is something that all politicians have dreamed of but have never dared to hope for.
I must confess that I am surprised to see subsection 2 of section 2 in the bill, coming as it does from the hon. member for York West, a member of the Progressive Conservative party. Hon. members will observe that the governor in council is authorized to prescribe for the violation of this section such penalties as he may deem necessary. The hon. gentleman is proposing that we pass an order in council.
In the learned and delicate manner in which this matter was handled by the hon. member for York West, he has taken a simple matter of pollution and worked it up so that it has reached the lofty pinnacle of human rights. That is no mean accomplishment. In view of the heights to which this pollution has risen, I would humbly suggest to the hon. member for York West that he withdraw this bill and make it a section of that bill which has been so often recommended to this house by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I should like to support this bill with regard to section 1. I think it would be a delightful thing if we had jurisdiction to deal with this matter. I am anxious to clear up this situation in the interests not only of my own constituency but of contiguous ridings. One cannot help sympathizing with the motive behind this bill. This matter of pollution is a nuisance, having been for generations injurious to health and in many other ways as well. Steps should be taken to remedy the situation. I cannot think of anything that is more necessary throughout the provinces of this country. As I suggested earlier, I do not feel that it is a matter for the parliament of Canada to deal with, but that opinion is again offered humbly and with respect.
I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, if we could not have the views of the Minister of Transport on this matter. He doubtless has a clear conception of the constitutionality of the bill


before the house. It would be a distinct pleasure to me to have his views if he sees fit to offer them at this time.

I have listened with interest, Mr. Speaker, to this debate which has been participated in by members on both sides of the house. I think there will be general agreement with the intention of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) and the purpose he had in mind when he introduced this bill. It is a laudable thing for the hon. member to seek to protect the waters of lake Ontario and those of other lakes and streams against pollution by oil and other chemical products. No one who has the interests of his constituents at heart wants to see the beaches-whether they be on lake Ontario or on any of our other lakes and streams-polluted to the extent to which the hon. gentleman has made reference. But, however laudable is the intention of the hon. member for York West, there can be no doubt that there would not be the slightest use of attempting to find a remedy in a place which has no jurisdiction, to begin with, and never could have it in any sense of the word.
I said that I listened with interest to the debate which has taken place. I do not think I need to speak at great length because several of the members who have spoken have challenged the validity of this proposed act, even a member on the same side of the house as the hon. member for York West. I refer to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who is a lawyer and who I think immediately realized-as did the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Henderson) and the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter)-the futility of attempting, by the method suggested, to deal with a serious situation such as that complained about. I think my friend the hon. member for York West presented an excellent argument-and as I listened to him he piled up argument after argument-for provincial intervention, but certainly not for dominion intervention. He started off by saying that the amendment contained two principles. One was the protection of riparian rights. Surely the federal government has no jurisdiction with reference to riparian rights. It is a question of property and civil rights, which falls under the jurisdiction of the provinces.
The hon. member cited the case of McKie v. K.V.P., 1941, 1 D.L.R. at page 39, which is clear evidence against him that this is a matter for provincial, and not federal, jurisdiction. Then he went on to say that the real reason for introducing the bill was to do away with pollution of waters. Pollution is a matter which concerns health and therefore falls under the jurisdiction of the province.

I do not want to repeat what the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hunter), the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Henderson) and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) said, but let me summarize in one word if I may the legal argument, dealing with only one factual argument afterwards.
The hon. member seeks to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. That act is divided into three parts. The first part deals with works which are built in navigable waters and is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works. The second part concerns the protection, the obstruction, the interference and the impeding of navigation and is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport. The third part has to do with the installation of ferry cable crossings, swing bridges and the like, and is also under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport. The part with which we are concerned at the moment is part II, clearly that which concerns the protection of navigation. The whole intent of part II of the Navigable Waters Protection Act is to pi-otect navigation. The words say so. The whole intent of my hon. friend's bill is to do away with pollution. His bill clearly says so, or at least section 19 (1) does. I will not read it all because it is somewhat lengthy, but the governing words of section 19 (1) are these:
. . . which has the effect of polluting the water into which it enters or is liable to pollute such waters.
In one word the act deals with the protection of navigation, and in another word the bill deals with the pollution of waters. The latter is a matter of health and therefore is one falling under the jurisdiction of the provinces.
Subsection (2) is clearly ultra vires. It says:
No municipality with a population greater than three thousand shall discharge or permit the discharge by its officers, servants, or employees of raw sewage into navigable water or into any other water which flows into navigable water.
Section 92, paragraph 8, of the British North America Act states:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-
Municipal institutions in the province.
My hon. friend would want this parliament to legislate with reference to municipal institutions in the province. He provides in his bill for direction to the municipalities. Clearly that section is equally ultra vires. The same may be said of section 26A (1)- and I am repeating here the argument of the hon. member for Parkdale and the hon. member for Kingston City, when I maintain that section 26A (1) of the bill is straight interference with property and civil rights.
Navigable Waters Protection Act What right would the Minister of Transport have to direct or instruct the owners of provincial plants? What right would he have to place officers in those institutions, the direction over which lies with the provinces? It would be straight interference with property and civil rights. I think the same can be said of subsection 2 of section 26A (1), which would constitute another interference with municipal institutions.
The explanatory note of the bill indicates what the hon. gentleman had in mind. It states:
The purpose of this act is to control industrial plants and oil refineries situated on navigable waters, . . .
I submit with deference that this house has no jurisdiction to control industrial plants and oil refineries simply because they are situated on navigable water. We have certain jurisdiction over navigable waters by virtue of part II of the act. For instance, section 19 is intended to keep channels free of logs, sawdust, edgings, slabs and other things which may impede navigation; but in no sense can oil be said to impede navigation, certainly not in the sense that this bill contemplates. Then the explanatory note goes on to say:
... so that their operation does not result in the pollution of the surrounding water area and shore line.
The word "pollution" and the words, "shore line" clearly indicate to me that these are matters concerning property and civil rights and therefore come under provincial jurisdiction. The last sentence of the explanatory note reads:
These three new sections merely enlarge the scope of the original act . . .
This is not a true statement of fact. The three new sections do not merely enlarge the scope of the act; they change entirely the intention of the act. The act is for the protection of navigation; the bill deals with protection against pollution; therefore it is not an enlargement of the scope, it is a change in the nature of the act. The explanatory note goes on to say:
. . . which dealt solely with the pollution of navigable waters by sawmills.
The act does not deal with the pollution of navigable waters; it is concerned with navigation and the protection of navigation.
I do not think I need elaborate on the legal points any further. The hon. member will agree that the house is sympathetic toward him, and appreciates the feelings of the people who have suffered because of the pollution. But clearly this is not the forum where the remedy should be found.
The matter is one which has been of particular interest to me because in the city of Cornwall, whence I come, a similar situation

Navigable Waters Protection Act has arisen from time to time, and the position taken there was the same as that now taken.
It might interest the house to know that in 1946 the international joint commission was asked to consider the problem of pollution of waters in so far as they were international, and they were asked by the Department of Transport to undertake a survey of such waters in order to determine the factors responsible for pollution and to recommend appropriate steps to the respective governments of Canada and the United States, because it was felt at that time by myself and the officers of the department that this was far too important a question not to be given the best possible attention. For that reason the international joint commission, which was asked to take it under advisement, appointed an advisory board of eight technicians, four from Canada-two from the Department of National Health and Welfare and two from the provincial department of health of Ontario-and four from the United States.
The first part of this advisory board's report, covering the waters between lake Superior and lake Erie, will be presented to the international joint commission on October 12, 1949. The second section of their report, covering the waters between lake Erie and lake Ontario, is in the course of preparation and will not be available when the findings of the field staff are fully analysed. This survey, I need hardly say, concerns the pollution of international boundary waters from all causes and not from oil alone. Its terms of reference do not cover the bodies of water between lake Ontario and the end of the international section of the St. Lawrence river near Cornwall.
If it meets with the approval of the house I am perfectly willing to ask the international joint commission to add to its survey the additional international waters extending from the head of lake Ontario to the international boundary at Cornwall.
I think it will meet the wishes of all hon. members, in part at least, if a practical suggestion is made in regard to an attempt to assist those who have suffered by the pollution of waters. But to endeavour to do it by an act of this parliament or by this bill would be, I believe, a serious mistake, even if it could be done, which it cannot. Such legislation would be challenged immediately and I have no doubt would be declared ultra vires.
Therefore I have to inform the house that, for the reasons given, the government cannot accept this bill. I would hope that what I have said will meet the feeling of the house and that perhaps the hon. gentleman will be willing to withdraw his bill.
tMr. Chevrier.]

Mr. Speaker, before this debate closes I should like to say a few words. First, I wish to congratulate the hon. member upon having introduced this bill, bringing this important matter to the attention of the house and thereby to the attention of the country. This matter of pollution has been overlooked too long in many places in Canada up to the present time.
While I support the principle of the bill I quite agree with the legalistic argument of the minister as far as the jurisdiction of this house to pass this legislation is concerned. I do not think we can deal with this situation adequately until there is a national policy on pollution of rivers as a result of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. Therefore I do not think it is sufficient for the minister just to give a legalistic argument in reply to the hon. member who has introduced this bill.
I would point out to the minister that the present act deals with the pollution of navigable waters by saw mills, but even those provisions are not enforced. I should like the minister to tell the house at some time the procedure that is followed for the enforcement of those provisions in the act.

The procedure is to bring into operation sections 27 to 30 of the act which provide penalties for anyone who obstructs navigation contrary to the sections of part I of the act. Any person may proceed under those sections.

This question of navigable waters is a most interesting one because we get so many constitutional definitions. I have had navigable waters explained to me as being under the jurisdiction of the federal government in so far as they are being used for navigation, and as being under the jurisdiction of the provinces when they are being used for the development of power. So far I have not had any clear explanation of the jurisdiction that applies so far as pollution is concerned.
I might say that I wqs in the provincial legislature of British Columbia some years ago and at that time I brought up the question of the pollution of navigable waters. I was then told that it was a federal: matter. We certainly are not going to get anywhere with this matter by simply giving legal explanations for inaction. The only hope we can have of solving this question is through co-operation with the provinces. This is a most important matter in many parts of this country. When considering a problem I always like to find out what others have done and in this connection I

have read some United States literature. That country being older and more densely populated, the question has become more intense and serious. From what I read, the different states have had considerable difficulty in connection with the pollution of navigable and other waters. I should like to read to the house details of the policy that has been developed by Pennsylvania as the result of years of study and experience. Here is the policy now in effect in the state of Pennsylvania:
Under this, the streams of the country, upon the basis of their use in transporting sewage and industrial wastes, may be classified into three groups, as has been done by the sanitary water board of Pennsylvania:
Class A:	Relatively clean and pure streams.
Streams in their natural state probably subject to chance contamination by human beings but unpolluted or uncontaminated from any artificial source, hence generally fit for domestic water supply after chlorination, will support fish life and may be safely used for recreational purposes.
I recognize that in dealing with this question there has to be a compromise between theory and practice. I am giving the house these classifications because from what I have read I think they represent a proper compromise between theory and practice. I continue:
Class B: Streams in which pollution shall be controlled. Streams more or less polluted, where the extent of regulation, control, or elimination of pollution will be determined by a consideration of (a) The present and probable future use and condition of the stream; (b) The practicability of remedial measures for abatement of pollution; and (c) The general interests of the public through the protection of the public health, the health of animals, fish and aquatic life, and the use of the stream for recreational purposes.
Class C: Polluted streams. Streams now so polluted that they cannot be used as sources of public water supplies, will not support fish life and are not used for recreational purposes and also from the standpoint of the public interests and practicability it is not now necessary, economical, or advisable to attempt to restore them to a clean condition.
All artificial pollution of Class A streams is prohibited. Any sewage or industrial wastes on the watershed are to be treated to such a degree that the effluent shall be practically free from suspended matter, nonputrescent and disinfected. Recreational use shall not be sanctioned within prejudicial influence of waterworks' intakes.
The degree of treatment of sewage and industrial wastes discharged into Class B streams is to be determined for each particular stream or portion thereof after consideration of the general interests of the public and the economics of the particular case.
Sewage and industrial wastes may be discharged into Class C streams provided that they do not create a public nuisance or menace to health.
I have read that outline of classification as far as pollution of streams is concerned because I think it is the basis for a sound approach to the whole situation in Canada. I hope that, now the member has brought the matter to the attention of the house, some-
Navigable Waters Protection Act thing will be done about it. It is obviously a matter of great interest to quite a number of members, and I hope that the minister will explore the question beyond the legal aspect in order that it may be taken up with the provinces to see if something cannot be done, by co-operation between the provinces and the federal government, to develop a national policy regarding the pollution of navigable and other waters.
I understand that if I speak now I close the debate.
Yes.

In
closing the debate, may I say that I am grateful for the legal opinions offered by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). I do not disagree with him, but the original act simply refers to sawdust, edgings, slabs, bark or rubbish of any description whatsoever being discharged into any river or stream. Perhaps bark or slabs may be considered a menace to navigation, but certainly sawdust and rubbish cannot be considered any more a menace to navigation than oil slicks which, as has been pointed out, foul the bottoms of ships, create a considerable fire hazard, upset the internal operations of condensers for cooling water, thus making it impossible to obtain drinking water from the lakes, and in other ways interfere with the operation of ships.
I submit that the bill is intra vires because of the way section 19 now reads. However, I will not press that, because I am grateful to the minister for having suggested that the international joint commission will undertake a study of the matter of pollution. The Canadian members of the international joint commission were appointed by this house. At the present time they are studying and reporting on the subject of pollution although it is considered to be ultra vires of this house. I merely mention that as an example of the tortuous reasonings and difficulties that we get into on the constitutional question of whether a bill such as mine is ultra vires of the jurisdiction of the house.
Sewage disposal was mentioned by several members who seem to object to some treatment of raw sewage before it is discharged into the waters of the country. Let me say to them that eventually the discharging of raw sewage will be prohibited. Eventually an enlightened public opinion will see to it that raw sewage is treated. My suggestion was that a start should be made at once because the longer it goes on, and the larger the cities grow, the more difficult the solution of the problem will be.

Meat Packing Industry
I had hoped that the bill might be sent to the railway committee where experts on the matter of pollution, people who know the problem, and interested industrialists could get together and give evidence from which a suitable bill might have been evolved and presented to the house. That is not the wish of the government, however, so that cannot happen. I think it is a pity because, despite the question of jurisdiction, despite the legal arguments, the members of this house are sent here to protect the interests of their constituents. I feel that the pollution of navigable waters not only creates a hazard to navigation for the reasons I have given, but also is a considerable menace to the people who live beside these navigable waters.
