subtopic: WORKS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, September 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North) for the second reading of Bill No. 5, to declare the meat packing industry works for the general advantage of Canada.

subtopic: WORKS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Before we proceed to vote on this measure to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act I want to say a few words. I believe that the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Winnipeg North is of great importance not only to the meat packing industry but to Canada as a whole. I believe it can be regarded as a bill which is in line with words used in the British North America Act, "for the peace, order and good government of Canada." Its object of course is to take into consideration that part of the meat packing industry that carries on operations in two or more provinces, subject of course to paragraph (c) of section 53 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and therefore to give parliament the right to intervene in disputes of nation-wide importance. Section 92 of the British North America Act sets out the powers conferred upon the provinces at confederation. In my reading of the English language and the act, not placing a strictly legalistic interpretation upon the words, it seems to me it was clearly intended that provincial legislatures should have jurisdiction over all matters of provincial interest. Paragraph 10 states this very clearly, when it excepts:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:

Then, as hon. members will remember, it enumerates undertakings which clearly cut across provincial boundaries and are indeed of national consequence. For example, it states:
Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the prqvince.
Then subparagraph (c) adds this:
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
At the time of confederation there was no meat packing industry as we understand it today. Under conditions then existing the community was served by many small butcher shops. The butcher slaughtered the cattle and served the community with the meat. He was in close relationship wilh the agricultural producer, the farmer, whom he usually knew and from whom he bought his cattle; and he knew the members of the community who would buy at his shop. That was the situation some eighty years ago. In this country today, however, as in the United States and some other countries, that primitive butchering industry has given way to a nation-wide packing industry. In our own country we not only find that industry nation-wide; in the main we find it in the hands of three great companies. There are smaller packing concerns, of course, but the dominant companies in that field are Canada Packers, Swift Canadian and Burns Limited. Those three companies employ thousands of people from one end of this country to the other. They purchase their livestock not directly from the farmers but largely through commission agents in a few large centres. In the same way their products are sold all across the country through various agencies. So the industry is entirely different from that which was known at the time of confederation.
From my reading of the debates and of what transpired at that time. I believe the fathers of confederation saw that there might be an evolution in this country and that, in the process of such evolution, undertakings, as they put it, which at that time were of local significance serving only a community or a province, might be extended to become something much greater and much wider. So they put in section 92 the words to which I have referred, which I believe have a bearing on this discussion. No longer is the farmer dependent upon an understanding with the local butcher for the marketing of his animals. He ships them great distances. In my own province they are shipped to

Moose Jaw, Saskatoon and Regina; and often the farmer ships them beyond the boundaries of his own province, to Winnipeg, east to Toronto, and so on. So anything which interferes with the operation of that industry, not only in individual localities but from one end of the country to the other, seriously embarrasses the farmer. We discovered that in 1947, when a dispute between these companies and their employees held up the marketing of stock which was ready for the market, and caused not only serious inconvenience to the agricultural community but serious loss to agricultural producers. In the same way and at the same time the consumers who were dependent upon this nation-wide industry were also greatly embarrassed by the shortage of meat which occurred during the strike. As for the men engaged in the industry, organized in a nation-wide union rather than in provincial units of a union, they were denied the wages upon which they depended for their livelihood, and the whole matter was such that it caused serious difficulty all across the country.
During the war years and subsequently, in 1945 and 1946, when similar disputes occurred, they could be negotiated and a settlement assisted under federal jurisdiction, but in 1947 there was no such federal authority. The strike was prolonged, and the packing house workers were compelled to negotiate in the various provinces. As a result the farmer lost, the worker lost, and the community suffered grave inconvenience. So I say this industry is no longer a matter of purely local interest. It is of nation-wide concern; and I believe this parliament should do as it did in the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company some time ago

declare this an industry of national importance and therefore coming under the legislation to which I have just referred.
As I said a few moments ago, this is a matter of nation-wide concern; and if I can read the English language it seems clear that it would certainly fall under subparagraph (c) of subsection 10 of section 92, which declares:
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province-
Then I omit the words I read previously: -declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
With our experience in 1945 and 1946, when the Department of Labour, acting under legislation passed by this parliament and powers granted by this parliament, had the right to assist in the negotiation and settlement of such disputes, so today in peacetime, if the same situation arises, because of the
Meat Packing Industry same national considerations dealing with a nation-wide industry, we believe the same good offices should be exercised by the federal authority.
I do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to prolong the debate. I merely rose to say that in our opinion and in the opinion of the employees organized in the packing house industry, in the interests of the agricultural community and the consumers of Canada generally who are, of course, vitally affected when a dispute arises in an industry of this nation-wide significance, we should adopt the amendment suggested in Bill No. 5. This would enable our Department of Labour to assist in negotiations which may be necessary from time to time between the employees and the owners of the meat packing industry, which we contend is of nation-wide concern and of nation-wide importance, and thus should be subject to nation-wide jurisdiction.

subtopic: WORKS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before a vote is taken on this bill, I should like to say a word or two. It is not my intention to speak for long or to hold up the bill at all. It does seem to me that the bill is suggesting a change which would affect the provinces materially. So far as I am aware, none of the provinces have complained or asked for co-operation from the federal government in the management of its labour relations with the packing industry.
It is my view that this legislation does come within the purview of the provinces. Until such time as the provinces have made a request for dominion government assistance or co-operation in having this industry brought under the national labour code, I cannot see where benefits would flow from our interference with the relationship as it exists today. I believe the matter should remain as it is until the provinces make such a request. I am a little suspicious, Mr. Speaker, of centralizing any power of this character. I can see a great danger to labour and to the country generally in it. There is too much centralization at Ottawa now. For the reasons I have given, although I am not going further into them now, I shall have to vote against the bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: WORKS AND UNDERTAKINGS DECLARED TO BE FOR THE GENERAL ADVANTAGE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I rise to speak for a few moments because of the argument advanced by the member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston). It is an argument that has been advanced by others who have taken part in this debate, namely, that there has been no formal request from the provinces for this particular change. It seems to me that argument is another example of waiting until after the horse is stolen before locking the barn door. The fact

Meat Packing Industry of the matter is that, during the last serious dispute in the packing house industry, a number of provinces did request federal government assistance in conciliation. One of the difficulties at that time was that the provinces were not unanimous in asking the federal government to take over the matter, and this prevented effective action at the proper time. If we are going to use wisdom in the matter, surely that experience would lead us to make preparations for future disputes of this kind. It does seem to me that the arguments that have been put forward as to the nation-wide character of this industry and the argument advanced by my leader as to the interest in this matter on the part of consumers, workers in the packing house industry and our farmers who produce the livestock, make an affirmative vote by members of this house the part of wisdom.
At this time, I should like to deal with an argument advanced the other night by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll). The last time this bill was before the house the discussion hinged largely on the constitutional point. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond even went so far as to contend there was a difference in value between section 92, 10 (a) and section 92, 10 (c) of the British North America Act. He argued that the federal parliament did not have as much power under section 92, 10 (c) as under section 92, 10 (a). As I have often had to remark, I am not a lawyer, but it does seem to me to be clear, even from such law as I have learned sitting in this house, that if this parliament has a power assigned to it by the British North America Act it has all the powers that flow therefrom. If this government is assigned the powers set out in section 92, 10 (c), which have been quoted a number of times, we have the powers that flow from it.
Parliament has used that power a number of times. Grain elevators have been declared works for the general advantage of Canada. A similar declaration was made with regard to the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. Two or three years ago a bill was passed in connection with the Quebec, North Shore and Labrador railway in which a clause was inserted making it a work for the general advantage of Canada. Reference has already been made during the course of this debate to the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company whose property is astride the Manitoba-Saskatchewan boundary; its works were declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. In all of these cases the federal parliament has exercised its power as provided by the constitution. When members rise in this debate, as they have, and [DOT]contend that this would be opening the door,

they fail to remember that the door is already open. The suggestions of my leader have been carried out and there has been a recognition of the fact that times have changed since 1867. Some of the things the fathers of confederation did not know would come into existence are here today, and we have in some respects tried to keep up with the times.
Since this matter was up the last time, I was interested in discovering a reference to possible uses to be made of section 92, 10 (c) of the British North America Act, which is found in volume 2 of the report of the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, generally known as the Rowell-Sirois report, at page 201. This section deals generally with the problem of railway and highway competition and the commissioners indicate the kind of use that might be made of section 92, 10 (c). I want to quote this paragraph:
The situation may, however, not be permanent since main motor highways might possibly be brought under dominion jurisdiction under section 92, subsection 10, of the British North America Act, which provided that local works and undertakings wholly situate within a province may be declared by parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada or of two or more provinces. By the exercise of the declaratory power, parliament attained jurisdiction over many railways wholly situated within a province, and over grain elevators. While the term "works'' awaits definite judicial definition, there would seem to be no reason why it would not cover highways of the type indicated. Thus, Hon. Mr. Meighen, while the proposed transport act was being considered by the senate standing committee, February 10, 1937, said: "It would not be unreasonable to declare that the trans-Canada highway was a work for the general advantage of Canada."
I quote that to indicate that it is recognized that the door is open wherever it is desirable or necessary to bring under federal jurisdiction undertakings that are of nation-wide importance.
I should like to mention another point in that connection, and that is that in the labour code itself the language in section 92, 10 (c) of the British North America Act is quoted. Then, we go one step further in the labour code, which is chapter 54 of the statutes of 1948, by this enactment in section 54:
Part I of this act shall apply in respect of any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada and in respect of employees of such corporation, except any such corporation, and the employees thereof, that the governor in council excludes from the provisions of part I.
I do not know what action has been taken under that section with regard to the Polymer Corporation at Sarnia, where we make synthetic rubber. But unless the governor in council has excepted it from the provisions of this act, it is a crown corporation and as such comes under the provisions of the national labour code.

Some hon. members have said that this bill would bring a number of small local plants under the provisions of the national labour code. Not so, because the bill proposed by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) applies only in the case where a meat-packing firm operates in two or more provinces.
It has been a bit of a spectacle to some of us sitting in this chamber to hear these constant emotional appeals to the concept of provincial rights. This is a bill to protect the rights of Canadians in all the provinces: surely that is more important than the autonomous rights of the provinces as separate units. To some of us these sectional appeals hardly seem to square with the stirring speeches we have heard during the course of this very session urging us to recognize our status as Canadians and to establish the greatness of our Canadian nationhood. Here is a chance to protect the rights of the people in the provinces, in particular the rights that are guaranteed to them by the national labour code brought in by this government, if only we will take this step and bring this nationwide industry under federal jurisdiction with regard to labour matters.

Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate because I feel that there are one or two points that have not been brought out, despite the fact that so far excellent reasons have been put forth by previous speakers for checking these crime comics to some extent and for passing Bill No. 10 to amend the Criminal Code. The following is a report of the findings of a committee appointed by the Peterborough home and school council, to determine whether there are objectionable comic books on sale in Peterborough and if so, what might be done to inhibit their distribution.
The committee visited several retail stores where comic books were sold and found a large variety on the stands of which about half were deemed harmful, in greater or less degree. According to the salesman, the retail proprietors do not order any specific comics. About once a week the distributor collects the slow moving copies for which he subsequently obtains credit and leaves a new supply.
The committee then visited the two local distributing agencies and were courteously received by the managers. It was found that at least ten of the Detroit police department's list of objectionable comics were being distributed in Peterborough along with other crime comics.
There is more to the letter, but I will not read it all. It was sent to me by the corresponding secretary of the home and school council of the city of Peterborough. Here is a list, compiled by the detective bureau of the Detroit police department, of crime 45781-37J

For a moment I should like to refer to the bill itself, though I do not wish to be unduly critical of the draftsmanship. The bill refers to the printing, publishing, sale and distribution of any magazine, periodical or book. The word "magazine" indicates to me a publication containing sketches, stories and essays. Surely crime comics do not come within that definition. A "periodical" conveys to my mind a publication appearing at fixed intervals of more than one day, and I feel that crime comics do not come within the scope of that definition. The word "book" conveys to my mind a printed volume bound between two covers, and I do not think that would include crime comics either. I may be construing this bill rather strictly, but in view of the fact that if it is adopted it will be interpreted strictly in some other place, I believe we should scrutinize it carefully here. I am wondering whether these crime comics, as we understand them, are really covered by the expressions used in the bill. It may be that this is not so. speechtext: The hon. member says it is for charity. It seems to me it is stretching the idea of charity rather far when buying a ticket on a game of chance is considered a contribution to charity. No one buys a ticket on a lottery, a game of chance or competition unless he expects to get more back than he pays for the ticket; that does not seem to me to be charity. Charity is what you give even to your own inconvenience, when it hurts it is not giving with the expectation of getting back more than you gave. I have heard all these arguments before. We are told that lotteries for worthy objects are all right. If the object is worthy, it should not have to depend on a lottery. If it is not worthy, it should not be supported at all.

It has everything to do with this bill because the bill suggests an amendment to the Criminal Code. I am suggesting that if one section of the Criminal Code is not enforced, perhaps this amended section will not be enforced either.
There is another point in connection with this matter that I want to mention. Before I deal with that, however, may I say that it is a rather saddening experience to pass a newsstand today and see the amount of trash offered for sale and the very small amount of literature that is worth while. I do not believe we can overcome the effects of crime comics merely by negative action. If the lives of our young people are to be improved, it will have to be by positive action. Something constructive for them to do will have to be found; something that will take up their time so that they will not have time for crime comics and other harmful diversions. When most of the members of this house were growing up there was not much time for comic papers. I suppose a good many of us grew up on the farm, where there was always work to do. If it did not do anything else, at least it kept us out of mischief. On that same basis, I suggest that, if we are going to improve the lives of our children and youth of today, we must put something in their lives to fill the emptiness that is the lot of so many.
It is evident that the member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) does not agree with that. It is his belief that crime can be suppressed by courts and laws.
I said, "How are you going to do that with all these gift shops?"

If history has proven anything at all, it has proven that crime cannot be stopped in that way.
I have only one more remark to make before I sit down. I shall listen attentively to the constructive suggestions that will be made by the voluble member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard). I think perhaps we can say too much about the harmfulness of crime comics. Perhaps we may be just advertising them. The other night when the member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and the member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) were talking, I felt that clergymen should not talk about these things because they build such an alluring halo around them that it makes people think that resisting temptation is not worth while. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the member

for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) on the excellent job he made when presenting this bill. So far as its principle is concerned, I shall support it.

In this particular I want to give a great deal of credit to the Rev. Gordon Domm of Bathurst street United church for taking these young people off the streets of the district, opening the basement of his church to them, and doing a great deal of rehabilitation work. I do not think that sufficient appreciation has ever been shown of the work that he and his committee have done. There is one remarkable aspect of this matter of juvenile delinquency and the extraordinary variety of anti-social behaviour that is going on today. It is a wild and extraordinarily imaginative type, caused in part by these crime magazines but also in part by the daily press. When some strange and violent incidents of anti-social behaviour took place in Toronto, it was found that the daily press of Toronto played them up-I do not intend to mention the incidents, but they have occurred from week to week-with the names, the description, the location and all the rest of it. That practice made heroes of these young delinquents who committed these peculiar manifestations of anti-social behaviour. I would rather call them that than crimes, although they are crimes.
When this was publicized-and it was particularly so in groups and gangs-people would say, "Oh, well, look what they did over there. They have done this particular thing." That gave the incentive for another group to go and do some other even worse act in another part of the city. This cannot be anything but a plea to the daily press, when these anti-social incidents occur, when these peculiar acts of sadism and violence that are all too common today in Canada occur, not to play up the participants as heroes. I know that they have tremendous news value. I know that the newspapers depend on the sale of their papers, and the circulation depends on news value and news interest in the papers; but I do plead with the daily press and the weekly press that when these extraordinary things occur they do not give them publicity, because it merely sets the pattern for others to try to emulate.
I know that it is asking a lot of the press. It is something that they can only do voluntarily. I am speaking as a member of the committee on the beanery gang, and I know that when the press stopped playing up the delinquent actions in Toronto the concentration of members gradually decreased. It is a matter of example, and if the daily press

will display restraint in emphasizing the bad examples I am sure that a great deal of good can be done.

I repeat that in this country and on this North American continent there is a tremendous dearth of literature for young people. In this connection we owe a debt, but of the wrong sort, to our United States friends. Our imitation of them is a part of the inferiority complex which Canada has developed. The result is that we have not gone into the field of literature for youth or indeed into any field of literature with outstanding success. It is certainly true that there is nothing in this country for the young people to read as compared with what is available to young people in other countries, particularly in Great Britain. In that country there is a great choice of reading matter for young people as well as for adults.
I suggest that instead of censorship or court action we institute a counter-attack by substituting things that are good for things that are evil. Trash.

Trash; that is a good name for it. I do not want to dignify it by calling it literature. It seems to me that there is one other point that ought to be stressed further.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) appeal to the newspapers about the whole problem. I think there is a responsibility on the part of the newspapers of the country not to overplay the gruesome and morbid details of crimes that are committed in reality. Our boys and girls cannot help reading the newspapers that come into our homes. Surely we ought not to feel that our journals and our newspapers are not fit for our boys and girls to read. I think we ought to encourage our boys and girls to read the papers, but any time a journalist writes up one of these crimes committed in society I think he should not play up the lewd and sensational in order to appeal to the morbid curiosity of readers. That in itself has a deteriorating effect on the mind of the child, and a child is quite likely to be tempted to try some of the things he hears about such as skinning victims alive from their necks up or down.
I saw a portrayal of that kind of thing in one of our daily newspapers. They are only trying to play up sensationalism. I add my voice to that of the hon. member for York West in appealing to the newspapers to try to play down that kind of thing as much as possible in order that our boys and girls will have something clean and decent to read in our daily and weekly newspapers.
I have come to the conclusion that we must attack this evil on all fronts. There is the positive approach, which the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has mentioned, and with which I agree. But it is not enough, just as it is not enough to try to

educate our people against the evils of overindulgence in liquor. We have to do something by way of legal control in order to keep as many as possible of our younger people away from it at least until they have reached the age of self-control and restraint. So I say it must be a double-barrelled approach; and for that reason I am congratulating the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) on his courage and responsible citizenship in bringing forward this bill, which we as a group intend to support.

It was not my intention this evening, Mr. Speaker, to add my voice to what seems to be the unanimous opinion of the house, but during the last few minutes of the debate a different note seems to have entered the discussion, a suggestion that our present system does not provide sufficient entertainment for our children and that this is probably why they carry on the reading of these crime comics in a quiet way, while not under the supervision of their parents.
That is an opinion with which I disagree wholeheartedly, and I am going to try to prove that such is not the case. I shall take as an example one child whom I know intimately; I refer to my daughter, who is ten years of age, and who has a number of companions of the same age. In the town in which I live I think it would be safe to say that from the beginning ninety to ninety-five per cent of the youngsters have had all the toys they could possibly play with, going from three-wheel tricycles until they reach high school and ride bicycles. They have had at their disposal swimming pools in the summer time and skating rinks in the winter; they have gone skiing and have had every other conceivable type of pastime. If they should be given any more entertainment you would have to take them by the hand and force them to play.
However, I have found it necessary to maintain a certain degree of censorship on the comic books that come into our home by the trading method. A child buys a book for ten cents; in a month he may buy twenty books, and all are circulated. The majority of them are entertaining and easy to read, but we have encountered some that certainly should not be seen by children of that age. The minds of these children are naturally wholesome, but if that type of material is continually shown them they are bound to read it some time or other, even if they have the strictest supervision in their homes. It is very unlikely that they would commit any of these crimes, but certainly it is good neither for their souls nor for their bodies to have this sort of stuff presented to them. Whatever our supervision may be, if a trap
(Mr. Low.]
is set on the lawn our children are very likely to fall into it. I believe the people who are setting these traps should be either put behind bars or given some other severe penalty. *

I rise to support this bill, Mr. Speaker, and to congratulate the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) on introducing it. I sincerely hope it does not meet the fate of the other private members' bills that have been introduced so far this session. Not being a lawyer, I do not know whether some bright legal light on the government side will find that this bill interferes with property and civil rights, or with other provincial rights. It may even be found that the federal government will have to spend some money to enforce this legislation when it becomes law, and it may be ruled out of order on that ground. Seriously, however, I hope it will receive the careful consideration of every hon. member of the house, that it will be considered on its merits, and that the government, if it is not prepared to accept the bill, at least will not do anything to bring about its defeat.
As has been stated already, I recognize that legislation in itself is no substitute for education, for good libraries or good literature. It is no substitute for healthful recreation or for good home training. I agree with everything that has been said with regard to the positive approach to this question. I think much more can and should be done by way of a positive approach; but the fact is that in a great many homes it is just about impossible for a child to get the sort of training some hon. members have mentioned, to which no doubt children are entitled. We have to accept conditions as they are. We do not have good libraries everywhere. There is a dearth of good reading material for boys and girls of the adolescent age.
I think we should bear in mind that every church organization, every educational institution, every cultural organization and as a matter of fact every organization interested in building good citizens is concerned with this problem; and I am quite sure this legislation will have the support of all those groups. While we may accept the fact that legislation is not a substitute for all those other things I have mentioned, while we may accept the fact that legislation without enforcement is useless or worse than useless, still I see no good reason why we should deplore the possibility of obtaining enforcement of this legislation. I am quite sure public opinion against crime comics in this country is sufficient to warrant the application and enforcement of such legislation as we have before us this evening.

1 believe the question we must keep in mind is this. Why should we permit a few publishers or distributors of this kind of literature to go on day in and day out, undoing and undermining the very thing the churches, educational institutions and cultural organizations of this country are trying to build? Why is it necessary for us to permit these papers to be sold just for the sake of the profit there is in this business? Surely we can, by legislation, lend our support to those who are fighting this battle. We can do that by accepting this bill.
On motion of Mr. Tustin the debate was adjourned.

He said:	Mr. Speaker, in introducing this
bill there are two things I want to say at the outset. First, I hope that it does not give rise to a debate on the merits or demerits of the port of Churchill so far as the physical capacities of that port are concerned. That is not my purpose in introducing the bill. There are many difficulties in marketing grain through the port of Churchill other than any physical handicaps that may exist at that port. I have introduced this bill for the purpose of removing what I, at least, believe to be an injustice existing in the financial arrangements for marketing wheat through that port.
When the port of Churchill was first talked about many years ago, the grain growers of western Canada were asking through their organizations for a railroad and a port at that point. The dominion government allotted certain lands in western Canada for the purpose of building that railroad. I believe some 14 million acres of land was sold for approximately $42 million. According to the minister of transport who spoke in this house on March 31, 1945 the Hudson Bay railway itself cost $32,500,000; the terminal works at Churchill $13 million; the terminal works at Nelson, which were afterwards abandoned, $6 million: a total of fifty-one and one-half million. This money was western money set aside out of the sale of western land for the development of the port of Churchill. Naturally, the farmers in western Canada thought they would derive certain benefits from that port when it came into operation.
The producers of wheat in western Canada have received very little benefit from the port. Any benefit there may have been from shipping wheat through Churchill has
Canadian Wheat Board Act largely gone to the consumer rather than to the producer. I have before me a summary of the cost of shipping grain through the port of Churchill as compared with the various other routes. This table was compiled by the Hudson Bay Route Association, and I believe it is correct. For the great lakes route: first via lake and rail, it costs 58-037 cents per bushel; via all water to transfer points, 56-671 cents per bushel; via lake and rail to Halifax and Saint John, 59-605 cents per bushel. To ship wheat through Vancouver to England it costs 59-65 cents; through Churchill the cost is only 45 * 95 cents per bushel, leaving a favourable balance so far as Churchill is concerned of anywhere from ten to fourteen cents a bushel.
Up to date the wheat growers of western Canada have received no benefit from that lower rate. I will admit that this bill will not give that to us, but it will go part of the way. It is only a step. Whether or not the bill is accepted by the government depends perhaps on the government's intention with regard to the port of Churchill. I put on the order paper a question which was answered on September 29. The purpose of the question was to try to find out what the government's intention might be with regard to the port of Churchill and the marketing of wheat through that port under the world wheat agreement. Until now, we have shipped wheat through the port of Churchill under the British wheat agreement and sold it at the same price as we received at Fort William or Port Arthur. I asked the following question:
Has the wheat board established a price for wheat at Churchill under the world wheat agreement?
The answer was:
No, but question was raised and matter is receiving attention.
I do not know whether it has received that attention and the government has arrived at any decision. Perhaps the minister will give us some information on that when he speaks on this bill. Until some consideration is given with respect to the price at Churchill as compared with Port Arthur and Fort William, the people in western Canada who allocated some 14 million acres of land and spent approximately $42 million for the building of that railway will not derive any benefit from it.
This bill has been introduced for the purpose of eliminating what I believe to be an injustice. In 1940 when the Wheat Board Act was amended the word "Vancouver" was added wherever the words "Port Arthur and Fort William" appeared. Before that amendment, the people living in the western part of Saskatchewan and the province of Alberta were paid for their wheat on the basis of

Canadian Wheat Board Act the Port Arthur-Fort William price less the freight from the point of delivery. After that amendment to the wheat board act those people whose freight rate to Vancouver was less than the freight rate to Port Arthur or Fort William were paid for their wheat on the basis of the Vancouver freight rate.
During the war, the wheat board took delivery of that wheat and, although little wheat was shipped through the port of Vancouver and most of it was taken to Port Arthur and Fort William, the difference between the freight rate to Vancouver and the freight rate to Port Arthur-Fort William was paid out of the general funds of the board. It was an equalization measure and, so far as the remainder of the growers were concerned, the freight rate was equalized. The people who live in northern Saskatchewan and northern Manitoba find the freight rate to the port of Churchill is lower than the rate to Port Arthur-Fort William. It is my belief that those people should receive the benefit of that lower rate structure, and that is the reason for the introduction of this bill.
There is not as great a differential in the freight rate to Churchill as there is in the freight rate to Vancouver. As a matter of fact, if we take Hudson Bay junction as being the point at which wheat from northern Saskatchewan will go either to Port Arthur or Churchill, we find the freight rate from Hudson Bay junction to Port Arthur is 21 cents per hundred. The freight rate to Churchill is 18 cents per hundred. This leaves a difference of 3 cents that those people would receive in the form of an increased price for wheat because of that lower rate to Churchill. If the freight rate were equalized, however, on the basis of miles, the differential would be greater.
The mileage from Hudson Bay junction to Churchill is 598-6 miles and to Fort William and Port Arthur it is 816-5 miles. Worked out on an equalized mileage rate this would mean that the freight rate from Hudson Bay junction to Port Arthur or Fort William should be 15-6 cents per hundred rather than the 18 cents. Again, if the railroad construction program which should be carried out in northern Saskatchewan were completed, and if those roads which were started towards the port of Churchill or towards The Pas in Manitoba to connect up with the Hudson Bay railway were completed-that is, from Nipa-win north, from Carrot River and Arborfield north to The Pas-that would reduce the mileage again so that there would be a reasonable advantage in the freight rate to Churchill as compared with the freight rate to Port Arthur and Fort William. We in that part of Saskatchewan feel that, if the people in IMr. Wright.]
western Saskatchewan and Alberta are tc receive the benefit of the lower freight rate to Vancouver, we should be entitled to the lower freight rate to Churchill.
The minister may say that that 3 cents that is there at the present time does nol amount to anything, and that the diversion charge that is made by the grain company eats up the advantage that there is in the freight rate. That argument is right at the present time. Personally I think it is time that we did something about these diversion charges. For instance, I see no reason why companies handling the farmers' grain, especially where they are shipping it to a point where they have no terminal elevators of their own, should charge 1J cents a bushel for diverting that grain to that particular point. That is what happens at the present time. Whatever justice there may be in the elevator companies making this diversion charge where the wheat is going to Port Arthur and Fort William where they have a terminal of their own, in which this wheat could be placed, when the wheat is placed in a terminal elevator other than their own and a diversion charge of 1| cents a bushel is made, I certainly cannot see any justice in that. As a matter of fact, I do not think they should make that charge at all. I do not think it is justified. At the present time that diversion charge is there.
But even though that diversion charge is there, if this bill were to pass it would mean -as it has been interpreted to me, at least- that the favourable freight rate would be paid on all grain grown in that area even though it did not go to Churchill, and that we would get paid for our wheat on the basis of the more favourable freight rate to Churchill even though that grain went to Port Arthur or Fort William. That is what is happening in western' Saskatchewan, and that is what is happening in Alberta where they are paid on the basis of the Vancouver freight rate structure there.
There is just one point which I hope the minister will clear up, and it is this. If it is the government's intention to make a different price on wheat out of Churchill in respect of the world wheat agreement, this bill might mean that the advantage which might be gained through that price could not be passed back to the farmers living in the favourable freight rate area adjacent to the port of Churchill. I do not want the bill to have that effect. That is not the intention of the bill. The intention of the bill is simply to provide that those people in the freight areas favourable to Churchill should have the same privileges as are enjoyed by those people in western Saskatchewan and Alberta with respect to the port of Vancouver.

It has been said that the port of Churchill an never handle a great deal of grain. To late I do not think there has been any year in which the port has handled much over 5 million bushels; in fact, it has only been for two or three years that 5 million bushels have been handled. But it is possible for the port to handle a great deal more, and I believe it will do so. Even the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has stated that. I just want to quote from Hansard of the second session of 1945, volume 1, page 1109, where the minister is reported as having stated:
In spite of the short season I think it may be possible to reach the objective of those who developed the route, which was a movement of 20,000,000 bushels of grain in the season. That does not sound much when compared with the movement through Port Arthur and Fort William or through Vancouver. but 20,000,000 bushels is a considerable movement for any port. Few ports on the continent have larger movements than that. Therefore I am not suggesting that the outlook for Churchill is hopeless; far from it. I feel that in post-war years the port will develop as far as its physical limitations will permit, and I can assure the house that the government will make every effort to see that that development is pressed actively and vigorously.
I submit that the passing of this bill would be one method of developing that port. It would mean that people living adjacent to the port would get the same advantage out of it. That is what they spent their money for. That is what the route was developed for, namely, to give some advantage to the people living in the west and more particularly, I believe, to those people in northern Manitoba and northern Saskatchewan who live adjacent to the port.

In actual practice grain is not shipped into Churchill in October and November. Shipments to Churchill begin in about May or June, and the elevator is filled to capacity when the shipping season actually opens. However, it is filled with grain that has

Canadian Wheat Board Act accumulated a carrying charge of perhaps only two months, at the maximum two or three months, instead of eleven months as would happen if the grain were moved into the elevator at this time. As X say, sufficient of the old crop is assembled to fill the elevator. Certain other old crop is held back to take care of the interval until the new crop begins to move, and then sufficient new crop is diverted into the elevator to take care of any boats that may be en route to that port. At the end of the season the elevator is empty. All the grain has been shipped, and the elevator remains empty until the following spring. As my hon. friend will appreciate, it is a closely regulated movement. It involves the minimum of storage and carrying charges and interest on the wheat. It is the kind of movement that is best for the grain growers of all Canada who pay all bills for the movement of wheat.

I mean economically possible. Another thing is that this is a short wheat crop. It is selling very readily. The crop is pretty well sold at this time, and it is sold for delivery within the current crop year. My hon. friend will appreciate that the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement ends at the end of this year, as does the five-year pool on wheat. Naturally it is greatly in the interests of Canada to deliver that wheat within the current crop year so that it may be delivered under the wheat agreement. I do not know what the price of wheat will be for the crop year 1950-51, and I am sure that my hon. friend does not know either. But if I were guessing I would guess that it might be a lower price than the price under the present contract. Well, if that wheat is in Churchill it cannot be delivered against the wheat contract, and therefore all the farmers in Canada would have to suffer a loss that would accrue through a price differential as between the next crop year and this crop year. There is a further difficulty that the wheat delivered during this year and shipped to Churchill is part of the wheat that must be accounted for under the contract. If that wheat were in Churchill the settlement under the five-year pool would have to be delayed until that wheat was actually marketed.
Those are the practical difficulties. There is another practical difficulty. Again I say I 
assume that my hon. friend would not wan1 a fictitious value put on wheat. He would want it based on actual possibilities. There are some 40 million bushels of wheat that are tributary to the port of Churchill. As far as price differentials are concerned, we all know that only a fraction of that 40 million bushels can possibly be shipped through Churchill, My hon. friend says the fraction may be 50 per cent. Actually under present day conditions it is not more than 12J per cent. Therefore 40 million bushels of wheat would benefit; whereas the actual movement that should properly benefit is the wheat which can actually move through the port which is only about 12J per cent of the wheat tributary to the port.
If the government were paying the bills one might say: "That is all right; justice demands that these payments shall be made. The government is a very indefinite person. He cannot complain very much. It is all the people of Canada." But it is not the government that is paying the bills; it is the producers of the prairie provinces. I would think that the grower who is not tributary to the port of Churchill would ask: Why should I be charged in order that those who theoretically can ship from Churchill shall all benefit through their proximity to that port?
Those are the objections. I think that they are very real objections. I believe that the best results for the port of Churchill can be obtained by allowing the wheat board, which I think everyone in this house will admit is doing a first rate job in looking after the interests of all the wheat growers of Canada, to handle grain to the port of Churchill in the interests of Canada, and in the interest of the grain growers of western Canada as a whole.
If there were no pool and if we had an open marketing system as we had years ago there would be no objection to allowing anyone to ship to the port of Churchill who wished to do so, provided the grain were sold as it used to be when it was loaded on a boat. If under those conditions a grower within the area wished to ship to Churchill in November, we will say, he would do so, but he would do so knowing that his grain must pay carrying charges, must pay storage and must pay interest until roughly the 1st of September of the year following. If they knew that, I am sure the people in that area would not ship. But if the proposal of my hon. friend were accepted, if Churchill were a basing point, the economics of the situation to the person in that area would disappear entirely. He would say: What do I care about the carrying charges or how much they are? I get


$1.75 when my grain goes into the elevator at Churchill, and I am going to ship it in November and let somebody else worry about when it comes out of the elevator. That would be a fictitious situation, a situation that would not follow the laws of economics, and a situation which I am sure my hon. friend would not care to foster.
Just to sum up. The differences between Churchill and Vancouver and Churchill and Port Arthur are, first, that only two or three grades of wheat are merchantable at Churchill. If my hon. friend put feed wheat into Churchill it would be there until someone railed it back to Le Pas and down to Port Arthur. In other words, it is a limited market. Second, it differs from the other ports in that it is open only about two and a half months in the year instead of twelve months. Third, it depends on contracts made by the buyers of the wheat with one merchant shipping line. I believe that line is the only one that does business into Churchill.
All grain there is at the risk of these contracts being made. Under present-day conditions wheat is not shipped until contracts have been made which specify grade, quantities and tonnage. My hon. friend will say that everyone should have confidence that those contracts can be made, but there is that element of uncertainty which is not present in the method of handling grain through the other ports.
While my hon. friend is seeking to remedy what he feels is an injustice to the grain growers within a particular radius of Churchill through not having Churchill as a basing point, his remedy would inflict a greater injustice upon the grain growers outside that radius who would have to pay the bills to enable the farmers to collect higher prices through the basing point being at Churchill.

I have a copy of a letter from the manager of the port in which he says that the facilities there would permit them to ship 25 million bushels out of the port so long as those facilities were not interfered with by too much in the way of imports. While we are working now under definite agreements, I submit that the minister's argument will not be as valid when those agreements run out. It has not always been as easy to sell wheat as it is today or as it was during the war years and the years just subsequent.
Is it not quite true that it is likely wheat will have to be stored at some point? It seems to me that it would not matter very much from an expense point of view where it is stored. I know that the wheat board gave instructions that October 6 should be the final date for shipments to Churchill, and I would not think there would be any large amount of wheat stored at that port this winter. The day will come when wheat will have to be stored.
I do not see any sense in taking delivery of all grain in the east any more than I could see any sense in the wheat board taking delivery of nearly all Saskatchewan flaxseed last year at Fort William. The result was that those people in Saskatchewan who wanted to crush flax could not get a kernel of grain lately. They would have had to haul it back to the prairie provinces.
I suggest that if wheat is going to be stored in preparation for shipment some of it might be stored in the government elevator at Saskatoon. As far as I am concerned that elevator is just a white elephant, because it stands year after year with the bins empty. Grain has often been stored on the farm, and I think that is a good policy, but more use should be made of the government storage elevators in various parts of the country.
I was disappointed, and I know the people in my constituency were disappointed, when the vegetable oil mill had to close down two or three weeks sooner than it ordinarily would because no flaxseed was stored at Saskatoon. I make a plea to the minister that if wheat has to be stored it should be stored at Churchill, and in the government elevator at Saskatoon which has a 5J million bushel capacity. I am going to keep on advocating the use of the port of Churchill. I should like the route to be tried at least once to full capacity. Give that port a chance to show what it can do.

Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) say that he had a special interest in Churchill. Many of us in northern Saskatchewan have a special interest in that port. After listening to the

Canadian Wheat Board Act minister a few minutes ago we realize that there are many ramifications in connection with the shipment of wheat through Churchill.
Early this fall we were much concerned over what we heard and read about the boats coming into Churchill having no grain to take out on their return trips. After hearing the minister speak tonight I am beginning to see the reason why there was no grain at the terminal at Saskatoon. We are also very much interested in that elevator, and I am particularly because my farm is not far from it.
The marketing of grain is of much concern to us all and the minister has said that it must be got out quickly on demand. Possibly that has much to do with there being no grain in the terminal at Saskatoon. I am hoping that in the future, when the marketing of our grain is in a more stable position than at the present time, greater use will be made of this port. I do not intend to say much more about the shipping of our grain, but I should like to read a letter which I received since coming down here which refers to Churchill. This letter has nothing to do with wheat, but I think its contents are significant. It is addressed to myself and reads:
It is my intention to bring some pedigreed cattle over from Great Britain next summer. Would prefer to ship into the country via the port of Churchill on account of that port being about 1,200 miles closer to our point than Halifax, thereby saving a long rail haul and consequently larger cost for freight, et cetera. At present there are no quarantine facilities at Churchill nor stockyards either (these were removed during the war) and it would be necessary to have quarantine facilities arranged by the Department of Agriculture, health of animals branch. Dr. Childs of Ottawa, I believe, is the chief veterinarian in charge of this.
He goes on to say:
I have discussed this matter with the secretary of the On to the Bay Association who is in correspondence with Messrs. Dalgleish, the shipping firm of Newcastle, who, for the past several years, have been sending ships to Churchill for wheat, with a view to ascertaining rates, etc., for transportation.
That letter is signed by P. J. Ibbotson, of Radisson, Sask. He happens to be a breeder of purebred Shorthorn cattle in my constituency, and also a grain grower. Such a letter does bring it to our attention that possibly greater use should be made of the port of Churchill, not only for the shipping of grain from Canada, but also for the shipping of livestock and goods from Great Britain to different parts of Canada.

The people of northern Saskatchewan and others fairly close to the port of Churchill should be able to take advantage of it, and are entitled to some benefits on account of its existence. If it is not feasible to put the necessary changes into effect this year then action should be taken as soon as possible so that the people adjacent to that port can reap those benefits. I believe I had something to do with having the port of Vancouver amendment made in the Canadian Wheat Board Act. In my opinion, while we were entitled to have that change made, others are also entitled to have the port of Churchill used as a basic port.
Therefore, while the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as I said before, has based most of his arguments on the short crop this year and the fact that our contract with Great Britain expires next year, I feel that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will have to get busy and see that we get more rain so that we can grow larger crops and use the port of Churchill as a storage port if for no other purpose. While he is doing that, the Minister of Trade and Commerce can see to it that we have a contract that will bring us beneficial results for the delivery of the wheat that we can produce provided we get the necessary rain.

I must say that I think the answers of the minister are rather weak. His whole case is predicated on the fact that the bill does not provide for the handling of the 40 million bushels of wheat that might be grown in the favourable freight rate area adjacent to Churchill. I think that argument may be wrong. With very little expansion the facilities at the port could be made to handle 40 million bushels of wheat. On the average, I do not think there are 40 million bushels of wheat produced in that area of the grades that can be marketed through Churchill. I think probably 25 million or 30 million would be closer to the amount that could be marketed from that area via the port of Churchill. Therefore I do not think his argument is sound.
His other argument is that if the freight rates were paid on the basis of all we produce in that area the growers in the area would not be interested in whether their wheat went to the port of Churchill because they would get the advantage even if it went to Port Arthur or Fort William. I should like to point out as to that argument that at the present time the wheat board-and I am not criticizing them because I think they have done a good job in many respects-have not put forth every effort to use the port of Churchill because it did not matter to the wheat board whether or not the wheat went there. They paid for it on the basis of the Fort William-Port Arthur price. If they had been paying for it on the basis of the Churchill price they would have been more interested in seeing that as much of that wheat as possible was delivered through the port of Churchill, either under the British contract or otherwise.
As for the minister's argument that wheat going to Churchill would remain in storage there until it had accumulated considerable storage charges against it, I should like to point out that in my memory there has not been a crop year in western Canada when there was not a carryover of wheat of anywhere from 40 million to as high as 400 or 500 million bushels. Therefore the two and a half million bushels of wheat that might be carried over at the port of Churchill would be a very small portion at any time of the total carryover of wheat in Canada. Carrying charges must be paid on that wheat whether it is at Churchill, Saskatoon, Fort William or Montreal. Carrying charges are accumulating just the same. I do not think the argument is sound that it is going to cost the wheat growers of the west a lot of money for carrying charges at the port of Churchill. As for its costing the wheat growers of western Canada more money because of the favourable freight rate to Churchill being
Canadian Wheat Board Act paid to the growers in the Churchill area, that depends entirely on whether we make full use of the port. I think that we can make full use of the port to the extent of the wheat that is grown in that area of the grades that can be marketed through Churchill.
The minister did not answer my inquiry as to what the possible price might be at Churchill under the world wheat contract. Possibly he cannot do so at the present time, but if a favourable price is obtained for wheat at the port of Churchill under the world contract, a price in excess of the price at Port Arthur or Fort William, then I think it is doubly necessary that the people adjacent to that port should get some advantage from that price.

subtopic: ALLOWANCES TO PERSONS SUFFERING INJURY, ACCIDENT OR CONGENITAL INFIRMITY
ALLOWANCES TO PERSONS SUFFERING INJURY, ACCIDENT OR CONGENITAL INFIRMITY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should during the present session take into consideration the advisability of including in their social security program a system of allowances to every person, without any sufficient income or means of support, who, by reason of an injury, accident, congenital infirmity or incurable disease, is at a disadvantage in seeking or obtaining employment, or incapable of providing for his subsistence, and whose age prevents him from benefiting by the social security legislation now in force.
He said: This motion was discussed in 1946 but was not adopted. It barely needs comment. My remarks will be very brief, because I should like to know the opinion of the house on this question. In 1946 no less than 15 hon. members, representing all parties in the house, supported the motion.

Social Security
The then Minister of National Health and Welfare also was sympathetic to it, and I have no doubt the present minister will be sympathetic as well. Numerous welfare associations supported such legislation at that time, and today they strongly urge its adoption.
In the domain of social security, Canada has made an effort which deserves mention. Family allowances are now enabling large families with low incomes to face the heavy charges imposed upon them by a higher cost of living. Indigent mothers, blind and aged people are receiving from various governments grants which alleviate their sufferings and permit them to improve their lives. Allowances and pensions give veterans an opportunity to rebuild their lives on a better basis and assure them of a living if, physically speaking, they have left parts of themselves in the conflict. The labourer temporarily out of work may realize unemployment insurance benefits.
Family allowances stop at the age of sixteen; old age pensions start at seventy. In my opinion the age limit for this latter pension should be lowered to sixty-five as soon as possible. The difference of fifty-four years between the ages of sixteen and seventy represents more than the average human life. In my opinion a certain section of the people within those age limits has been left unprovided for; that is, the invalids and cripples. This group includes the victims of infantile paralysis, those who have suffered accidents of all kinds but who do not come under the benefits of any provincial accident insurance, persons suffering from congenital deformities, and other sick people we cannot cure.
If these people or their families are wealthy they can obtain all the necessary treatments in peaceful surroundings, thus alleviating the burden of their misfortunes. If they are poor they have to rely upon public charity. No municipal bylaw will provide help for them; no provincial allowance, as far as I know, can give them any grant; and I could not discover any federal statute under which they might get assistance of any kind. No one will employ an invalid; he is not accepted on the labour market. In this age of mechanization the machine, which does not stop, supersedes the human who, in order to follow it, must have strong arms, strong legs and powerful eyesight. Invalids and crippled persons are set aside for reasons of security and production. In the meantime the cripples and invalids, out of work or occasionally employed at casual jobs, cannot earn their living. If they have wives and children their fate is simply tragic. Then they must resort to public charity or welfare associations, or

even beg from door to door. In addition to their physical misfortune they must undergo the brutal obligation of living desperate days with no hope of improvement. From week to week, under the heavy existence they have to bear, they become discouraged, if not filled with despair. Misfortune will poison them, but misery will kill them.
Crippled persons and invalids deserve their place in the sun. They have a right to happiness just the same as anyone else. So would it not be right for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr.-Martin) to study this problem and make a statement concerning these indigent persons, and then recommend a suitable system of allowances to be paid by the federal government or subsidized by both the federal and provincial authorities? The social security program cannot be complete if indigent invalids and crippled persons are left to their unfortunate fate.
Everyone endorses a program of social security for children, for the family, for indigent mothers, for the aged and blind, and for veterans and disabled soldiers. I am sure everyone will also endorse a movement to extend to crippled people and invalids the total sympathy of the nation, if special legislation to that effect is presented. Their existence on a lounge chair is restricted by the horizon of their window. They live in darkness, without light or company, in a state of perpetual restlessness with respect to the future, constant dejection, sleepless nights and continuous disappointment. A person who has never suffered cannot understand the darkness cast upon the life of a hapless person afflicted with infirmity, want and often poverty. Let us assure them that even though they may be ignored locally the nation as a whole is not indifferent to their fate and will not reject them from our national life. Spreading joy means spreading peace. To abolish social misery means strengthening the security of the nation.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, everyone approves the social security granted to children, families, indigent mothers, old men and women, blind persons, veterans and disabled servicemen. Everyone will also express approval if we extend to cripples and invalids the full sympathy of the nation, under the form of legislation specially meant for them. Their outlook is limited to what they can see through the window from their lounge-chair; it is restricted to a house whose threshold definitely shuts out the horizon; it is concentrated in the shadows, because they dread sunlight and the crowds; it centres around a

succession of worries about the future, of endless discouragement, of sleepless nights and of accumulated despair. Those who have never suffered cannot realize how gloomy is the solitary life of the hapless people who have to contend with physical disability, want and too often distress. Let us cast some ray of hope in their direction, by helping them to live. Let us give them the assurance that, while they may be unknown and unnoticed locally, the nation as a whole is not unmindful of their plight and does not consider them as outcasts. By giving joy we ensure peace; and by abolishing social distress we strengthen the security of the nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution now before the house commends itself to the sympathy and attention of all members. I am sure they appreciate the humanitarian views of the sponsor of this resolution who is bringing the matter before us for the fourth time. I have no doubt his views are shared by all members of this house. The welfare of the masses is the concern of all right-thinking citizens since no state can progress in harmony nor can a democratic society develop unless the vast majority of the people can live without fear and anxiety. The need of man is to live in security and freedom; not only political freedom which we in this country are fortunate enough to enjoy-often without realizing our good fortune-but freedom from want and freedom from fear of what tomorrow may have in store for us.
It was for this reason that years ago, under Liberal guidance, this country embarked on a program of social security. It has developed gradually, step by step, bringing joy to so many families, bread and better clothing to so many children throughout the country by means of the family allowances. That perfection has not yet been attained, I would be the first to admit, but I should not like my friends opposite to overlook the propriety of giving justice where justice is due. I am, of course, referring to the administration that has given Canada a system of social security of which we might well be proud even though, as I said before, it is not perfect.
If I may be permitted to quote a few words I said in this house in 1946, which are to be found at page 738 of Hansard:
Social security is not a cure-all for man's troubles, nor is it intended to prevent man from working for his living. It would not be right to bring into being any social system which would have as its outcome any diminution, if I may so describe it, of individual effort, or any crushing of initiative. On the other hand, it is impossible to do away with risks and responsibilities, and it would not be right to have a society based on paternalism. What must
Social Security
be created is equality of opportunity for all. Heredity, talent, initiative and work will soon make sure that equality of attainment will not be achieved.
In principle, sir, all men are born equal; yet from the moment of their conception they are unequal. Some are born of healthy parents and some are born invalids, diseased and sick. Some men are born of parents who have great intelligence, while others are born of less intelligent parents; some are born wealthy and others are born in poverty. The moment a man is born, inequality is born. A system of social security is needed to correct somewhat that situation which nature and life bring about in society. It is also a false principle that equal work brings equal results. We know too well that that is false.
The measure now before us proposes a pension for invalids. It has been argued by many economists and sociologists that such a measure should be adopted at the same time as health insurance. I should like, at this point, to put on the record what I said on this question of health insurance, which is found at page 740 of Hansard of 1946:
Sickness Is the most constant and frequent risk for the low income population and for wage earners in general. It is a risk which may entail the loss of health and earning capacity, the loss of livelihood, the loss of ability to pay for medical assistance.
What is needed is to place at the disposal of the people the facilities of modern medicine for the preservation of the health and detection of disease. As stated in the proposals to the provinces, under our present system, for those who cannot afford to pay, the cost of ill health falls at the very moment when earning capacity is cut off. Those unable to pay are left to the charity of benefactors. It is evident that a scheme of health insurance such as is proposed by the dominion to the provinces is necessary, and it is to be hoped that an agreement in this regard will be reached. Any such scheme should include an extension of assistance to the blind, assistance to needy mothers, and maternity grants.
And of course pensions for invalids. One of the most important aspects of social security is that which has to do with financial aid for interruptions or stoppage of income, or inability to earn sufficient income due to invalidity. The main headings under which such interruptions in work might be classified are unemployment, illness, age, disability and invalidity. Invalidity would fall into two different categories, temporary or permanent. There is also the question of industrial disability. The people who would suffer under this classification would be protected, of course, by the workmen's compensation acts that have been passed by the provinces. There are several classes of people who are not industrial invalids but who have been invalids from birth or who have never fallen into the category of people who were insured under the unemployment insurance scheme or who could not qualify
